review_basis: Original SAP Module 01 numbered WebP slides individually inspected, with diagrams and actual examples followed in display order.
part_title: Workforce Federation, Identity Center, SAML, SCIM and OIDC Trust

scenes.title: One identity, different account access
scenes.visual_overview: An enterprise directory connects to IAM Identity Center through distinct SAML sign-in and SCIM provisioning paths, then assigns different permissions in development and production accounts.
visual_walkthrough: Enterprise directory on left
SAML 2.0 authenticates while SCIM synchronizes users and groups
IAM Identity Center as federation hub
Permission set plus assignment points to development and production with different privileges
scenes.visual_example: The same engineer gets developer permissions in a development account and read-only access in production through separate assignments.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Authentication proves identity; account assignments and permission sets determine AWS access.
scenes.narration: This slide shows how one enterprise identity can receive different AWS permissions across accounts. Begin at the company directory on the left. Follow the upper path labelled SAML 2.0: it is used for federated sign-in, confirming the employee's identity. The lower path labelled SCIM is different; it provisions and synchronizes user and group records. Both lead to IAM Identity Center in the middle. On the right, a permission set and account assignment determine what that person can do in each AWS account. The example gives developer permissions in the development account but read-only permissions in production. The person does not need unrelated permanent IAM user keys in every account. Note that a permission set describes access, while an assignment connects that access to an account and user or group. For architecture scenarios, distinguish authentication and lifecycle provisioning from authorization. A successful corporate sign-in alone does not entitle a user to every AWS account.

scenes.title: SAML proves workforce sign-in
scenes.visual_overview: A four-stage federation process shows employee authentication at the enterprise identity provider, signed SAML assertion validation by Identity Center and a separately authorized AWS session.
visual_walkthrough: Employee signs in to enterprise identity provider
IdP issues signed SAML assertion
IAM Identity Center validates assertion and federated sign-in
AWS account session depends on permission set and assignment
scenes.visual_example: An employee signs in successfully through the company identity provider but sees only AWS accounts assigned through Identity Center.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A valid signed assertion authenticates identity; account access remains a separate authorization decision.
scenes.narration: This sequence explains what SAML does in workforce federation. Start with the employee on the left, signing in at the enterprise identity provider. The identity provider authenticates the person and issues a signed SAML assertion. The next arrow delivers this assertion for validation by IAM Identity Center, where configured trust and assertion details must match. The fourth panel shows the employee receiving an AWS account session, but only for an account and permission set to which the identity has been assigned. That final step is easy to overlook. The assertion confirms who the employee is; it does not simply grant administrator rights across the organization. In a troubleshooting case, if login fails, inspect the identity provider, SAML configuration, and assertion validation. If login succeeds but an account is absent or permissions are wrong, inspect Identity Center assignments and permission sets. The two outcomes involve different controls.

scenes.title: SCIM manages the identity lifecycle
scenes.visual_overview: Join, move and leave events in the enterprise directory synchronize identities and groups using SCIM, while SAML handles sign-in and account assignments remain separate.
visual_walkthrough: Join, move and leave events in enterprise directory
SCIM pathway provisions users and groups into Identity Center
SAML sign-in separately handles authentication
Account assignments lead to Accounts A, B and C
Leave event changes membership and future access, with explicit warning that SCIM does not create assignments
scenes.visual_example: A person moves teams; SCIM synchronizes updated group membership, but effective AWS access still depends on separately maintained assignments.
scenes.visual_synthesis: SCIM handles provisioning, SAML handles authentication, and Identity Center assignments govern account access.
scenes.narration: This slide adds lifecycle management to the identity architecture. On the left are three employee events: join, move, and leave. Follow the upper arrow into SCIM, the provisioning mechanism that synchronizes users and groups from the enterprise directory into IAM Identity Center. Follow the lower arrow into SAML sign-in, which is the separate authentication path. The right side shows accounts A, B, and C, where group and permission-set assignments determine access. A new employee might be provisioned successfully yet still have no AWS account assignment. Likewise, when someone changes departments, their synchronized group membership may change which assignments apply, but SCIM itself does not create those account assignments. On departure, deprovisioning and group removal reduce future access; active sessions and other credentials may still require additional revocation controls. The banner at the bottom gives the exam distinction: provisioning is not the same as authentication or authorization.

scenes.title: OIDC trust is more than a signed token
scenes.visual_overview: An external OIDC issuer presents a signed token containing issuer, audience and subject claims, and an IAM role trust policy checks the intended identity before STS returns credentials.
visual_walkthrough: External OIDC issuer at left
Token JSON includes iss, aud and sub claims
Trust policy checks matching issuer, audience and subject
Green result yields temporary credentials; mismatch follows red deny path
scenes.visual_example: A Kubernetes service-account token for team:app must not be able to assume a role configured for a different application identity.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Verify token validity and issuer trust, and tightly scope audience and subject conditions to prevent unintended federation.
scenes.narration: This diagram explains why a signed OIDC token is not sufficient on its own for assuming an AWS role. Begin with the external issuer on the left. It produces a signed token whose claims include iss, the issuer, aud, the intended audience, and sub, the subject identity. Move to the trust policy in the middle. AWS must trust the configured identity provider and validate the token; the role's trust conditions can then require the expected audience and precise subject. In the pictured example, the subject is a particular Kubernetes service account, team app. If the issuer, audience and subject meet the configured checks, STS can issue temporary role credentials. The red branch shows that a token targeting another audience or subject is rejected. This is particularly important for workloads in Kubernetes or external CI platforms. Don't rely solely on a valid signature. Bind the role to the exact issuer, intended token audience and permitted workload identity, then scope the role's permissions.

scenes.title: Choose federation by who is signing in
scenes.visual_overview: A four-row decision comparison maps employee, customer, application-client and on-premises certificate cases to distinct identity services.
visual_walkthrough: Employees across AWS accounts point to IAM Identity Center
Customer app sign-in points to Cognito user pool
Application needing direct AWS API access points to Cognito identity pool
On-premises server with X.509 certificate points to IAM Roles Anywhere
scenes.visual_example: An employee accesses multiple AWS accounts through Identity Center, while a customer logs in through a Cognito user pool and a certificate-based server can use Roles Anywhere.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Choose by the identity and credential problem rather than treating all federation technologies as interchangeable.
scenes.narration: This slide is a service-selection comparison, not a four-step workflow. Read each row from left to right. Employees accessing several AWS accounts belong in a workforce access design, typically IAM Identity Center. Customers signing into a web or mobile application use a customer identity service such as a Cognito user pool. If an application client requires direct AWS API credentials, a Cognito identity pool can broker limited temporary role credentials after supported authentication. The fourth row is different again: a server outside AWS with an X.509 certificate can use IAM Roles Anywhere to obtain temporary AWS role credentials, subject to configured trust and profile controls. The sentence at the bottom separates authentication, application authorization and AWS credential issuance. An application sign-in token is not itself an IAM access key. When answering a professional exam question, first ask whether the actor is a workforce user, an app customer, an AWS-API-calling client, or an external server, then choose the corresponding access pattern.
